newsitem.title: UK: Mideast/Japan VLCCs at year high, plateau seen.
newsitem.headline: Mideast/Japan VLCCs at year high, plateau seen.

text.p: Very large crude carrier (VLCC) rates to Japan and South Korea remained at their year high on Friday but brokers said they may have reached their peak.

"Although our tonnage forecast for the next four weeks indicates a slight reduction in availability to 35 vessels of about 10.6 million tons, it would be over-optimistic not to expect the pace of activity to slow a little which could moderate expectations of further improvements," said E.A. Gibson in their weekly tanker report.
Galbraith's Ltd broadly agreed, although it did not rule out the possibility of fixtures in the W80s for modern vessels.
"Generally however, the feeling is that we have just about reached the plateau for the time being.
"Tonnage for the first half of June is very thin on the ground, but then again there shouldn't be too many cargoes to fix in that period."

But they added: "The second half is a different story, more ships are of course available but owners of the more 'fixable' units have got 'the bit between their teeth' and are not likely to let charterers off the hook lightly."

West Africa/U.S. Gulf VLCCs, meanwhile, were steady at about W67.5, while the 310,000 tonne Settebello was fixed at W65 Sidi Kreir/UKC for Exxon. The Suezmax (130,000 tonne) market was flat with West Africa/U.S. voyages continuing to fetch about W92.5 and cross-Med trips W95.
The inter-U.K. Aframax (80,000 tonne) market has now lost the dynamism it showed last week when rates spiked up to around W140.
Vessels are now being fixed in the mid-W90s, and Galbraith's said: "The reason is very simple -- not enough business because of refinery and oilfield maintenance."

Galbraith's also pointed to the continued strength of the Caribbean Aframax market, where rates have averaged W201.88 over the last seven days. "Of course OPA (the U.S. Oil Pollution Act) and everything that goes with it accounts somewhat for the higher rates in the Caribbeans; equally the Mediterranean market is plagued with 'old ladies' while charterers in the Caribbean demand more modern ships. "But surely this massive disparity cannot continue," they added.
European fuel oil rates were unchanged, with 25,000 tonne cargoes at a strong W250 in the north but languishing around W190/200 in the Med.
